name: Russification
summary: Russification names the policies and processes, under the Russian Empire and the Soviet Union, by which non-Russians were pushed to adopt the Russian language and culture, together with the centralization that made Russian the language of administration and schooling. Scholars separate unplanned assimilation, administrative Russification and deliberate cultural assimilation, and stress that tsarist cultural assimilation was patchy while Soviet language spread was far more successful. Its documented practice includes bans on Ukrainian publishing, cuts to regional autonomy, resettlement of Russians into non-Russian republics and repression of national dissent. It states no positions on economics, gender, religion beyond the imperial context, or most other questions in the test.
scope: The policies and practice of Russification as the encyclopedias and Weeks define it: tsarist administrative and cultural Russification from the 1860s (Valuev circular, Ems Ukase, Poland, Finland, western provinces) and Soviet Russification of language and education. It excludes Russian nationalism in general, Sovietization as such, and post-Soviet Russian policy, which the defining sources treat as separate subjects.
